habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Spores ubiquitous in soil; can germinate in improperly canned/preserved low-acid foods
habitat.reservoir: Soil; contaminated home-canned or improperly preserved foods; honey (infant botulism)

microscopy.appearance: Gram-positive rods with subterminal spores ("tennis racket" appearance)

culture.media: Anaerobic blood agar, cooked meat broth

biochemicalTests.test: Toxin bioassay (mouse neutralization) or PCR for toxin genes
biochemicalTests.result: Positive for botulinum toxin genes/activity in toxigenic strains

identificationClues: Diagnosis is primarily clinical, confirmed by detecting botulinum toxin in serum, stool, or food, not by routine culture
Subterminal spores give a "tennis racket" appearance on Gram stain
History of home-canned/improperly preserved food, wound contamination, or (in infants) honey ingestion

diseases: Infant botulism (from ingested spores, not preformed toxin)
virulenceFactors: Botulinum neurotoxin (types A-G) — blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, causing flaccid paralysis
clinicalImportance.transmission: Ingestion of preformed toxin in improperly preserved food (foodborne); spore contamination of wounds (wound botulism); spore ingestion by infants, notably from honey (infant botulism)
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: Rare but medically urgent — foodborne botulism is a public health emergency requiring rapid antitoxin administration; infant botulism is why honey isn't recommended for children under 12 months
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Standard cultures don't establish the diagnosis — toxin detection (mouse bioassay historically, increasingly PCR/immunoassay) in serum, stool, or the suspect food is required

examFacts.importantTest: Toxin bioassay/immunoassay in serum, stool, or food
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release, causing descending flaccid paralysis — the opposite mechanism of tetanus toxin
